correctness.rationale: Pearson X-squared is exactly affine in the number of equal observation pairs. Conditioning one distinguished pair on equality versus inequality changes the expected additive cell statistic by precisely the binomial average of its second forward difference. The algebra gives the displayed coefficient. For the power-divergence family, strict convexity for positive lambda and strict concavity together with a negative normalization for minus one less than lambda less than zero give strict positive covariance; the lambda-zero limit is handled directly by k log k. The packaged enumeration reproduces the likelihood-ratio and representative power-family cases, and the quadratic specialization reproduces the exact Pearson variance.

evidence: Cressie--Read (1984) defines the power-divergence family and identifies Pearson and log likelihood as special cases; its published summary emphasizes asymptotic differences and finite-sample comparisons.

Marhuenda--Marhuenda--Morales (2003) treats the equiprobable multinomial case exactly, generating the support to compute exact marginal distributions, critical values, and powers for several divergence statistics.
Jann (2008) likewise treats exact small-sample tests by enumeration or Monte Carlo for Pearson, likelihood ratio, and the general power-divergence family.
broader_coverage.reasoning: These sources are broader in the choice of divergence and exact testing tasks, but the inspected statements and substantive sections do not supply the mixed covariance identity. Exact marginal distributions or separate critical values do not determine the joint covariance of two statistics on the same multinomial sample.

value.rationale: Pearson X-squared and the likelihood-ratio statistic are the two classical multinomial goodness-of-fit statistics, while the Cressie--Read family is the standard unifying class. The theorem gives an exact finite mechanism for their dependence: pair collisions probe only the discrete curvature of an additive cell score. This yields a universal sign theorem across all finite power divergences with lambda greater than minus one and clarifies why the Pearson and likelihood-ratio statistics align even before their common chi-square asymptotics become accurate. The result is structural and reusable for arbitrary additive cell statistics rather than a single numerical covariance.
